content.purpose: Read four facts off the prompt before typing anything, so you always know who you are and where you are.
content.mentalModel: The prompt is not decoration. In student@linuxlab:~$ the part before @ is your account, after @ is the machine's name, after : is the directory you are in, and the final character tells you your privilege level. A $ means an ordinary account. A # means you are root and nothing will stop you. Most damage done by beginners happens because they did not notice the character had changed.

demonstration.explanation: Confirms the account name shown before the @ in your prompt.
Prints the working directory in full. The prompt abbreviates your home directory to ~, and pwd shows what ~ stands for.

remember: student@linuxlab:~$ reads as account @ machine : directory, then a privilege marker
~ is shorthand for your home directory, /home/student
$ means an ordinary account, # means root

tasks.instruction: Confirm which account you are using and where you are. Run whoami, then pwd, then save the full path of your working directory into where-am-i.txt.

validators.message: where-am-i.txt does not contain your home directory path. Redirect the output of pwd into it.

hints: One command prints the working directory in full.
Send its output to a file with pwd > where-am-i.txt

tasks.instruction: Read the prompt below and explain to yourself what is different about it. Then prove you understand by creating a file called i-would-be-root.txt in your home directory.
tasks.diagnosis: Two things should have stopped you. The prompt ends in # rather than $, which means the session is root and no permission check will refuse the command. And the directory is / rather than ~, so a relative path would be interpreted from the top of the filesystem. Noticing the # is the habit worth building.
hints: Look at the character just before the space, and at the directory.

reviewQuestions.question: Your prompt reads analyst@linuxlab:/var/log#. What should concern you most?
answers: The # means this session is root
The account is analyst rather than student
Nothing: this is a normal prompt
reviewQuestions.explanation: The privilege marker matters more than the account or the directory, because as root nothing will refuse a destructive command.

reviewQuestions.question: Which command prints your working directory in full?
reviewQuestions.explanation: pwd stands for print working directory.
